questions.prompt: Arrange the reset steps given for this timing drill.

options.text: Return to the neutral-zone side of the right blue line.
Check that the coach has released the next action.
Continue the new support route while watching F1 and pressure.

questions.explanation: This sequence follows this exercise’s stated reset. It is not a substitute for learning the applicable full offside rule and its details.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example neutral-zone reset position behind the right blue line for this drill.
questions.explanation: The reference is on the neutral-zone side and gives YOU space separate from F1 and F2. It is an illustrative practice reset, not a geometric offside verdict about a skater’s feet.

questions.prompt: If F1 keeps waiting after YOU reset, what is the useful next check?

options.text: Cross early because F1 will probably move soon.
Check the coach’s release and time your next route with the puck.
Assume the practice condition has disappeared.

questions.explanation: The briefing makes the coach’s release part of this reset. Waiting or moving within the allowed space can be useful while YOU keep F1 and pressure in view.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between following this practice reset and making a full offside call.
questions.explanation: This exercise gives one location-and-release condition. A full rules decision needs the applicable rulebook and details such as the puck, skates and play context, which this simplified freeze does not establish.

title: Update the play when the coach stops the rep
objective: Recognize that a stated stop signal changes a loose-puck race into a controlled reset.
briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU and gold D1 had been approaching a loose puck in the neutral zone. The coach has just whistled and clearly called “stop this rep.” This is an explicit practice instruction. No official penalty or game stoppage is being inferred.
cues: The puck is still loose.
The coach explicitly stopped this practice rep.
Other skaters remain near the approach routes.

sources.title: USA Hockey: Skill Progressions for Youth Hockey
sources.section: 10-and-Under, printed pages 17–19 (PDF pages 23–25)
sources.use: Lists skill/team topics; Canadian adaptation and answers remain experimental.

limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. Age-level player knowledge and sportsmanship topics support listening and awareness. The static illustration cannot teach braking mechanics or certify a safe stopping distance. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: What has changed the task even though the puck remains loose?

options.text: Gold D1 has confirmed possession of the loose puck
The original race is still the active task
The coach has explicitly stopped this rep.

questions.explanation: The briefing gives the coach’s whistle and clear stop instruction. The puck is still unowned, but the current practice task is no longer to win the race.

questions.prompt: Which actions fit the stopped-rep instruction?

options.text: Stop competing for the puck and control your movement
Keep awareness of nearby skaters as you reset
Make one more challenge before listening

questions.explanation: The stopped rep calls for a controlled reset with awareness of others. A final challenge would continue the contest the coach has just ended. Technique and stopping room need on-ice instruction.

questions.prompt: Order this suggested response to the clear stop call.

options.text: Recognize the rep has ended.
Control movement while checking nearby skaters.
Listen for the next setup or coaching cue.

questions.explanation: The routine connects the signal to a controlled reset. It does not specify a braking technique or a distance every player can safely use.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example open reset location away from the loose-puck contest. Describe how you would get there under control.
questions.explanation: The reference separates YOU from the puck and D1’s current area. It is a reset destination for discussion, not proof of a safe immediate stopping path; actual speed, skill and other skaters matter.

questions.prompt: If the coach then restarts with F2 as the puck carrier, what should YOU confirm before beginning again?

options.text: Your new support role and the new puck situation
That the old loose-puck race still applies
That the old approach route is still open

questions.explanation: A new setup can give YOU a new responsibility. Confirm the coach’s instruction and current possession rather than carrying over the previous race.

questions.prompt: Why can the right decision change even when no player has touched the puck?
questions.explanation: The coach’s explicit instruction changed the task. Game information includes stated signals and constraints as well as puck location; here the useful response is a controlled reset and attention to the next instruction.
